entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jean d'Orléans-Longueville, born into a powerful cadet branch of the French royal House of Valois, emerged as a prominent ecclesiastical figure in early 16th-century France, culminating in his brief but significant elevation to cardinal in 1533. His career, spanning from his appointment as Archbishop of Toulouse in 1503 to his death just months after receiving the red hat, exemplifies the intertwining of aristocratic lineage, political influence, and high clerical office characteristic of the pre-Reformation Catholic Church in France. As a scion of the ducal house of Longueville, a family deeply entrenched in royal service and military command, his ascent within the Church was both a reflection of his family's prestige and a strategic consolidation of their power through ecclesiastical patronage, linking him directly to the French monarchy and its diplomatic ambitions.

Jean's ecclesiastical career began with substantial appointments, notably becoming Archbishop of Toulouse in 1503, a major metropolitan see, followed by his elevation to Bishop of Orléans in 1521. These roles were often held in commendam, allowing him to collect revenues while potentially delegating spiritual duties to suffragans. His most significant, albeit short-lived, achievement was his creation as a cardinal by Pope Clement VII on March 10, 1533, receiving the title of Cardinal-Priest of Santi Silvestro e Martino ai Monti. This elevation occurred during a period of intense diplomatic maneuvering between France, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Papacy, underscoring the political dimension of high clerical appointments.
